title: Chapter 2: Linux Foundations and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2)

blocks.text: Modern artificial intelligence, data engineering, and cloud backend deployments run almost exclusively on Linux. Whether deploying a machine learning microservice in a Kubernetes pod or compiling a high-throughput C++ binary, the operating environment is POSIX-compliant Linux. As a student on Windows, understanding the architecture of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) and mastering terminal fundamentals is your primary gateway to serious software development.
Operating System Architecture: Why Linux Matters
An operating system kernel acts as the arbiter between hardware resources (CPU, RAM, storage, network interfaces) and user applications.

blocks.caption: User Space versus Kernel Space separation in Linux.
blocks.alt: User Space versus Kernel Space separation in Linux.

blocks.text: In Windows, user-mode programs communicate with the Windows NT kernel via Win32 APIs and the Windows Executive. In Linux, applications invoke direct POSIX system calls (`syscalls`) such as `fork()`, `execve()`, and `mmap()`. Because machine learning libraries (such as PyTorch, OpenCV, and CUDA toolkits) and container runtimes (such as Docker) rely on low-level Linux kernel primitives—namely *namespaces* and *cgroups*—running them natively in Linux delivers maximum compatibility and performance.
WSL1 versus WSL2: Under the Hood
To provide Linux capabilities on Windows without requiring full-system dual-booting, Microsoft introduced the Windows Subsystem for Linux.

blocks.title: Key Highlights
lines: • **WSL1**: Utilized a translation layer. When a Linux binary executed a syscall like `fork()`, WSL1 intercepted the call and translated it on the fly into an equivalent NT kernel system call. This resulted in poor file system I/O performance and lacked support for Linux features like Docker daemon containers and complete CUDA device mapping.

• **WSL2**: Completely discarded translation. Instead, WSL2 executes a real, Microsoft-maintained Linux kernel inside a lightweight, highly optimized Hyper-V utility virtual machine. It boots in under one second, dynamically allocates RAM up to a configurable threshold, and supports 100% Linux system call compatibility.

blocks.text:
**The 9P Protocol & The Filesystem Performance Boundary:**
In WSL2, your Linux distribution (typically Ubuntu) stores its files inside a virtual hard disk (`ext4.vhdx`). When you access Windows files from Linux via the mount point `/mnt/c/`, traffic passes over the Plan 9 (9P) network file protocol. This incurs significant serialization overhead.
**Golden Rule**: Always store your Git repositories, Python virtual environments, and node_modules inside the Linux root filesystem (e.g., `~/projects/`), **not** inside `/mnt/c/Users/...`. Accessing Linux files inside `~` yields direct, native ext4 disk speeds ($>10\times$ faster).
The bash/zsh shell is a text-based command language and interpreter. Every engineer must possess muscle memory for standard filesystem, search, and process management operations.

blocks.code:
# Print Current Working Directory
pwd

# List directory contents with permissions, size, and hidden files
ls -la

# Change directory (relative, absolute, or home)
cd ~/projects
cd ..          # Move up one directory level
cd -           # Toggle back to previous directory

# Create nested directory trees
mkdir -p src/components/ui

# Create empty file or update timestamp
touch index.js

# Copy files and directories recursively
cp app.py app_backup.py
cp -r src/ src_backup/

# Move or rename files
mv old_name.cpp new_name.cpp
mv main.py ./src/

# Remove files and directories (use caution with -rf)
rm temp.log
rm -rf build/
blocks.caption: Core Filesystem Navigation and Management

blocks.text: Linux treats everything as a file, and processes communicate by chaining standard input (`stdin`), standard output (`stdout`), and standard error (`stderr`) using pipes (`|`).

blocks.code:
# Output entire file to terminal
cat config.json

# Read large files with paging (q to exit)
less dataset.csv

# View first/last N lines of a file
head -n 25 training.log
tail -n 50 training.log
tail -f training.log   # Continuously follow live logs

# Search recursively for a pattern, showing line numbers, ignoring binary
grep -rnI "API_KEY" ./src

# Count lines, words, and bytes
wc -l dataset.csv

# Chaining commands with pipes: Find errors and count occurrences
cat server.log | grep "ERROR" | wc -l

# Redirection: Overwrite (>) versus Append (>>)
echo "export PORT=8080" > .env
echo "export DEBUG=true" >> .env
blocks.caption: Stream Redirection and Text Processing

blocks.code:
# Display all running processes on the system
ps aux

# Search for a specific process PID
ps aux | grep python

# Real-time resource monitoring (CPU, RAM)
top
htop    # Interactive, readable process manager (install via apt)

# Terminate processes gracefully (SIGTERM) or forcefully (SIGKILL)
kill 14205         # SIGTERM (code 15)
kill -9 14205      # SIGKILL (code 9, non-catchable)
pkill -f "node"    # Kill by process name pattern

# Run a long job in the background and detach from terminal
nohup python3 train_model.py > train.log 2>&1 &
blocks.caption: Process Inspection and Management

blocks.text: In Linux, every file and directory possesses an owner, an associated group, and permission bits structured as `rwx` (Read=4, Write=2, Execute=1):

rows: Owner: Full; Group & Others: Read + Exec
blocks.caption: Standard Linux File Permission Octals.

blocks.code:
# Make a shell script executable
chmod +x build.sh

# Update package repository and install essential development tools
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y build-essential git curl wget python3-pip python3-venv
blocks.caption: Changing Permissions and Package Installation

blocks.text:
**Question**: *“Why are you compiling C++ and running Python in WSL2 instead of PowerShell directly on Windows?”*
**Defense**: *“WSL2 provides a true Linux kernel via Hyper-V virtualization. Linux provides identical memory allocation, glibc runtime behaviors, POSIX socket handling, and native package managers that match cloud production environments. Running on WSL2 ensures that our dev environment mirrors AWS/GCP servers and containerized Docker deployments, eliminating OS-specific drift.”*

**Pitfall: Windows CRLF vs. Linux LF Line Endings:**
Windows uses Carriage Return + Line Feed (`\ r\ n`), whereas Linux uses Line Feed only (`\ n`). If you create a Bash script on Windows or clone a repo with default Windows Git settings, running `./script.sh` inside WSL will fail with:
`/bin/bash^ M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory`.
**Fix**: Convert line endings using `dos2unix script.sh` or configure Git globally:
`git config –global core.autocrlf input`.

blocks.title: WSL2 \& Bash Mastery
blocks.text:
{Automated System Resource Watcher}
Write a bash script `syswatch.sh` that logs system uptime, available RAM in megabytes, top 3 memory-consuming processes, and saves the snapshot with an ISO-8601 timestamp into a log directory.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash, caption={System Health Monitoring Script (`syswatch.sh`)}]
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

LOG_DIR="$HOME/logs"
mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"
TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S")
LOG_FILE="$LOG_DIR/system_health_${TIMESTAMP}.log"

{
 echo "=========================================="
 echo "SYSTEM HEALTH REPORT: $TIMESTAMP"
 echo "Hostname: $(hostname) | Kernel: $(uname -r)"
 echo "=========================================="
 echo ""
 echo "— MEMORY USAGE (MB) —"
 free -m
 echo ""
 echo "— TOP 3 CPU CONSUMING PROCESSES —"
 ps aux –sort=-%cpu | head -n 4
 echo ""
 echo "— DISK SPACE USAGE —"
 df -h /
 echo "=========================================="
} > "$LOG_FILE"

echo "Report generated successfully at: $LOG_FILE"
\end{lstlisting}
